questions.q: Per this lesson, what three operational questions does Snowflake governance answer for every query?
options: Who can see this, what do they see once allowed, and what gets tracked when they look
How fast is the query, how much does it cost, and who wrote it
Which warehouse ran it, how long it took, and whether it was cached
Is the data fresh, is it backed up, and is it replicated
questions.explain: Governance in Snowflake is operational, not a policy document â€” it governs access, what's visible once access is granted, and auditability.

questions.q: What is Snowflake's full object hierarchy, from top to bottom, per this lesson?
options: Organization â†’ Account â†’ Database â†’ Schema â†’ Object
Account â†’ Organization â†’ Schema â†’ Database â†’ Object
Database â†’ Account â†’ Schema â†’ Object â†’ Organization
Organization â†’ Schema â†’ Account â†’ Database â†’ Object
questions.explain: Every object is namespaced through this chain: organization, then account, then database, then schema, then the object itself (a table, view, or governance object).

questions.q: Which role is automatically available to every user in a Snowflake account, with no explicit grant required?
options: SYSADMIN
PUBLIC
SECURITYADMIN
ACCOUNTADMIN
questions.explain: PUBLIC is the implicit base of the role hierarchy â€” every user has it automatically, no grant needed.

questions.q: In the Tasty Bytes example, which role creates tb_test_role, and which role grants it privileges?
options: SECURITYADMIN creates it; USERADMIN grants privileges
USERADMIN creates it; SECURITYADMIN grants privileges
ACCOUNTADMIN does both
SYSADMIN creates it; PUBLIC grants privileges
questions.explain: USERADMIN creates the role with CREATE OR REPLACE ROLE; SECURITYADMIN then grants it warehouse, database, and table privileges â€” a deliberate separation of duties.

questions.q: What does a dynamic data masking policy actually change about the underlying table when it's applied?
options: Nothing â€” the stored bytes stay exactly the same; only what a query returns changes
It permanently overwrites the sensitive columns with masked values
It deletes the sensitive columns entirely
It creates a second, permanently masked copy of the table
questions.explain: Dynamic masking is evaluated at query time. The table's stored data is untouched â€” Snowflake rewrites what a given query returns based on who's running it.

questions.q: What must be true about a masking policy's RETURNS type and the column it's attached to?
options: They must match exactly â€” a policy returning STRING can't be attached to a DATE column
They can be any compatible type, Snowflake converts automatically
RETURNS type only matters for numeric columns
There is no relationship between the two
questions.explain: A masking policy's RETURNS type must match the signature (val) type, and both must match the target column's data type â€” Snowflake needs the masked output to remain a legal value for that column.

questions.q: What does a row access policy control, as opposed to a masking policy?
options: Whether an entire row is visible to the querying role, not what a column's value looks like
Which warehouse a query runs on
How long a query is allowed to run
Which database a role can connect to
questions.explain: A row access policy is a boolean expression: TRUE means the row is visible, FALSE means it's silently filtered out. Masking policies, by contrast, change what a visible row's column values look like.

questions.q: What does a secure view hide that an ordinary view does not?
options: The row data returned by the view
The view's own SQL definition, from anyone without the privilege to see it
The name of the view itself
The warehouse used to query the view
questions.explain: By default, a view's SELECT statement is visible via SHOW VIEWS or GET_DDL even to those who can't query the underlying table. SECURE hides that definition from anyone without the right privilege.

questions.q: What does a tag do by itself, before anything is wired up to react to it?
options: Nothing to the data â€” it's pure governance metadata
It automatically masks the column it's applied to
It automatically restricts which roles can query the column
It deletes any data that doesn't match its ALLOWED_VALUES
questions.explain: A tag on its own is metadata only. What it enables (masking, reporting, discovery) depends entirely on what is wired up to react to it, as shown with masking policies in Lesson 10.

questions.q: What does SYSTEM$CLASSIFY_SCHEMA do that SYSTEM$CLASSIFY (applied to one table) does not?
options: Classifies and optionally auto-tags every table inside a named schema in one call
Deletes tags from every table in a schema
Applies a masking policy directly to every column in a schema
Only works on system tags, never custom tags
questions.explain: SYSTEM$CLASSIFY_SCHEMA runs the classification engine against every table in the named schema in a single call, rather than requiring one call per table.

questions.q: What does SYSTEM$CLASSIFY do by itself, without being wired to anything else?
options: Analyzes a table and recommends (and optionally applies) sensitivity tags â€” it does not mask data by itself
Automatically masks every column it identifies as sensitive
Deletes columns that contain sensitive data
Grants extra privileges to roles that need to see sensitive data
questions.explain: SYSTEM$CLASSIFY is a recommendation-and-tagging engine. It assigns system tags describing what a column is; masking only happens if a policy is separately wired to those tags, as in Lesson 10.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what distinct question do roles (Chapter 1) answer, as opposed to what tags and policies (Chapters 2-3) answer?
options: Roles decide who can do what; tags and policies decide what gets protected and how
Roles decide what gets protected; tags decide who can do what
Roles and tags answer the exact same question, just with different syntax
Roles only matter for warehouses; tags only matter for columns
questions.explain: The lesson's central framing: who (roles, Chapter 1) and what/how (masking, row policies, secure views, tags â€” Chapter 2-3) are two separate questions, and neither replaces the other.

questions.q: What does SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY log?
options: Every query executed in the account, including its text, user, role, status, and timing
Only queries that failed
Only DDL statements like CREATE and DROP
The current role hierarchy, not query activity
questions.explain: QUERY_HISTORY is a flat log of every statement that ran, regardless of type or outcome, with timing and status.

questions.q: What does GRANTS_TO_USERS show when filtered to deleted_on IS NULL?
options: Every currently active (not revoked) role grant, by user
Every query that ever contained a GRANT statement
Only grants made by the ACCOUNTADMIN role
Only grants made in the last 24 hours
questions.explain: GRANTS_TO_USERS is a point-in-time view of grant state; deleted_on IS NULL isolates grants that haven't been revoked.

questions.q: What three questions does this lesson say a real access audit has to answer?
options: Who touched the object, what they did to it, and when/how often
Which warehouse ran the query, its cost, and its duration
Which edition the account is on, its region, and its cloud provider
The table's row count, byte size, and clustering key
questions.explain: The lesson defines an audit as answering who, what (read/write), and when/how-often â€” turning a one-off curiosity into a real investigation.

questions.q: In Snowsight, what is a dashboard "tile" actually backed by?
options: A worksheet query, whose result set is rendered as a chart or table
A separate, dashboard-only query language distinct from SQL
A static image uploaded by the account administrator
A Snowpipe ingestion job
questions.explain: A tile is a worksheet's query result rendered visually â€” the same SQL you'd run directly in a worksheet, just saved and displayed on a dashboard.

questions.q: What happens when you run CREATE SHARE with no further statements?
options: Nothing is exposed to any other account â€” the share starts empty until objects are explicitly granted to it
The entire database becomes visible to every Snowflake account
A full copy of the database is created for sharing
All existing roles automatically gain access to the share
questions.explain: A share is empty by design on creation â€” visibility requires explicit GRANT statements naming exactly what's exposed.

questions.q: What does the DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS setting control?
options: How many days of Time Travel history are kept for an object before it moves to Fail-safe
How many days a user's password remains valid
How long a virtual warehouse stays running before auto-suspending
How many days a share remains active before expiring automatically
questions.explain: DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS is the governed policy for how far back Time Travel can query or restore an object.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that one Snowflake account is rarely a real company's whole picture?
options: Most organizations run multiple accounts â€” dev, test, production, sometimes per-region â€” and controls built in one are often forgotten in the next
Snowflake limits every organization to exactly one account by default
A single account cannot hold more than one database
Governance policies automatically apply account-wide with no configuration needed
questions.explain: Real organizations commonly have multiple accounts, and the risk this lesson highlights is a governance control (like a masking policy) being built once and not replicated when a new account appears.

questions.q: In this lesson's six-step checklist, what comes first, and why?
options: Creating a least-privilege role â€” access control has to exist before protection or classification mean anything
Sharing the data externally, so partners can start using it immediately
Dropping the table, to test Time Travel before anything else
Running the ACCESS_HISTORY audit query, before any policy exists to audit
questions.explain: The lesson's ordering starts with RBAC deliberately: masking, tagging, and auditing all assume access control is already in place as the foundation.
